title: Ash-e jow
subtitle: Persian barley and herb soup
excerpt: Ash-e jow is a thick Persian barley soup with chickpeas, lentils, spinach, and fresh herbs, finished with a squeeze of lemon. It is substantial enough to serve as a main course and is one of the most warming soups in the Iranian kitchen.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Ash-e jow documented as a classic Persian winter soup. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Notes on ash (thick Persian soups) as a category distinct from thinner soups.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. The barley thickens further on freezing; add a splash of water when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch. It keeps in the fridge for four days and improves over time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before. Reheat gently with extra water to loosen.

content.text: Ash-e jow is a thick Persian barley and legume soup with a generous amount of fresh herbs stirred in at the end. The barley makes it hearty and slightly gelatinous; the chickpeas and lentils add body. Turmeric and coriander give a warm, earthy base, and the herbs added at the end keep the flavour vivid. Serve with bread for a full meal.

Heat {{olive-oil}} in a large pot over medium heat. Add {{onion}} and cook for ten minutes until soft and golden. Stir in {{turmeric-ground}}, {{coriander-ground}}, and {{black-pepper}}. Cook for one minute.
Add {{pearl-barley}}, {{lentils-green}}, and 1.5 litres of water. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a simmer. Cover and cook for 30 minutes.
Add {{chickpeas-tinned}} and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Continue simmering for 20 minutes until the barley and lentils are very tender. Add more water if the soup becomes too thick.
Stir in {{spinach}}, {{parsley-flat}}, and {{coriander}}. Cook for three minutes until the spinach is wilted. Squeeze in lemon juice from {{lemon}}, taste, and adjust salt. Serve hot.

items.symptom: The soup is very thick and stodgy
items.cause: Barley has absorbed a lot of liquid
items.fix: Thin with boiling water from the kettle, adding 100 ml at a time. Ash is supposed to be thick but should still be spoonable.

items.symptom: The lentils are still firm after 30 minutes
items.cause: Not enough heat or old lentils
items.fix: Increase the heat slightly and cook for another ten minutes. Green lentils take 30 to 40 minutes to fully soften.
Add the spinach and fresh herbs only in the last three minutes. This keeps them vivid green and fresh-tasting.
Add salt and more lemon juice at the end. The lemon is essential: it lifts the earthy barley and legume base.

content.text: Ash is the Persian term for a category of thick soups, distinct from the thinner shorba. Ash-e jow (jow means barley) is one of the most common, eaten throughout the winter months. Persian ash is a social food: it is cooked in large quantities for communal gatherings, neighbourhood gatherings, and religious occasions. The combination of legumes and grain makes it nutritionally complete as a meal, and its origins are in the cooking of a culture where meat was not always available. The soup is topped with a drizzle of fried onion and dried mint in many households, which adds a final aromatic note.
